### The Lanternback of Veyra

At first glance, a lanternback looks like a small hill that has decided to go somewhere.

It lives on Veyra, a cold planet circling a dim red star. Most of Veyra’s surface is covered in shallow, dark seas, interrupted by chains of volcanic islands. Beneath a thick atmosphere, daylight resembles a cloudy evening on Earth. Plants grow almost black to absorb as much light as possible, and many animals make their own illumination.

The lanternback is one of the brightest.

### What it looks like

An adult lanternback is about four meters long and stands as high as a horse, though its body is broad and low. Six jointed legs spread beneath it, each ending in three soft, splayed toes. The toes can spread even farther when the animal crosses mud, distributing its weight like snowshoes.

Its skin is blue-gray, rubbery, and densely folded around the joints. Along its flanks hang fine silver filaments. These are sensory organs: they detect air currents, changes in temperature, and vibrations traveling through water. A lanternback standing ankle-deep in a pool can sense another animal approaching from the opposite bank without seeing it.

Its head is small, tucked beneath the front of its body. Four glossy eyes sit in a semicircle above a round mouth. Two eyes watch the ground, while the other two tilt upward to spot predators drifting through the low clouds.

Instead of teeth, the mouth contains overlapping mineral plates. These scrape food from rocks and crush the tough shells of small shoreline creatures. A long, violet tongue, divided into three flexible tips, sorts edible material from grit.

But its most striking feature is its back.

Seven translucent towers rise from its spine, the tallest nearly a meter high. They resemble hollow antlers made of smoky glass. Inside each tower, branching tissues hold colonies of glowing microorganisms. Their light shifts slowly between amber, green, and pale blue, depending on the chemical mixture supplied by the lanternback.

A relaxed animal shines a soft green. A frightened one flashes sharp blue pulses. During courtship, waves of amber travel from its head to its tail.

### What it eats

Lanternbacks graze along the edges of warm volcanic pools, feeding mainly on leathery mats of microbial life. These mats obtain energy from chemicals dissolved in the water, so they grow even during Veyra’s long winter nights.

The animal peels them off in strips with its mouth plates, then stores them in a fermentation chamber deep inside its torso. Communities of digestive microbes break down the tough material over several days.

This diet produces considerable heat. A lanternback’s body remains warm even when frost forms on its skin.

Its glowing back towers serve a practical purpose here: they are radiators. Warm blood flows through fine channels near their surfaces, shedding excess heat. In extreme cold, valves reduce that flow, and the towers become dim.

The light is useful too. Tiny flying animals gather around the glow, and some lay eggs in moist grooves at the towers’ bases. The lanternback periodically sweeps these grooves with its tongue, eating the eggs and larvae as a source of protein.

### How it spends its days

Lanternbacks live in loose herds of eight to twenty individuals. They do not have a permanent leader. Instead, whichever animal remembers the best feeding ground for the current season usually walks at the front.

A typical day begins with the herd emerging from a sheltered hollow where everyone has slept pressed flank to flank. The animals stand quietly while their towers warm and brighten. Then they walk toward the shore, following routes worn into the stone by generations of broad feet.

They feed slowly, often remaining in one pool for hours.

While grazing, they communicate through low vibrations made by muscular chambers in their chests. Humans would feel many of these calls through their feet rather than hear them. A short tremor means “move closer.” A rolling series of pulses announces a rich patch of food.

Their lights add information. A green flicker traveling down one side of the body can direct attention toward that side. Herd members often pause with their towers blinking in similar rhythms, maintaining contact through the mist.

### How it survives danger

The lanternback’s chief predator is the sailjaw, a light-bodied hunter that rides Veyra’s dense air on broad membranes.

When one appears overhead, the herd bunches together with the youngest animals in the center. Adults lower their heads and angle their glassy towers outward. The towers look delicate, but their walls contain layers of flexible protein reinforced with mineral fibers. They can bend under a blow without shattering.

At the same time, every adult flashes blue.

The sudden synchronized glare makes it difficult for a descending predator to judge distance. If the sailjaw continues its attack, the lanternbacks release a hot, bitter-smelling vapor from vents beneath their towers. The vapor irritates the predator’s sensitive flight membranes.

A lanternback rarely runs. On slippery volcanic shores, standing together is safer.

### How it raises its young

Once every three local years, adults gather at mineral-rich nesting grounds. After mating, each egg-bearing parent lays two or three soft-shelled eggs in warm gravel near a geothermal seep.

The parents take turns tending the nest. With their three-tipped tongues, they rotate the eggs, remove fungal growth, and adjust the gravel covering them. They also dribble water over the nest when it begins to dry.

The young hatch after several months. Each is about the size of a rabbit, with oversized feet and seven soft knobs along its back.

For their first weeks, the young eat a nutrient-rich secretion produced in folds beneath a parent’s neck. This secretion also supplies the microbes needed for digestion. Later, adults lead them to shallow feeding pools and scrape loose the softest food.

The back towers begin to grow in the first year. At first they are dark. The glowing microorganisms are transferred when a youngster rubs its developing towers against those of an adult.

For a few nights afterward, its lights blink irregularly as the colonies establish themselves. Then they settle into a steady green.

### Its place in the world

Lanternbacks reshape Veyra’s shorelines simply by living there. Their grazing prevents microbial mats from smothering entire pools. Their footprints become nurseries for small aquatic animals, and their dung carries nutrients from the sea onto barren volcanic ground.

They may live for sixty Earth years. Older individuals can be recognized by their cloudy, scarred towers and the pale streaks around their eyes. They often remember safe routes to warm water when volcanic activity changes, and other herd members follow them across unfamiliar ground.

From a distant cliff, a migrating herd looks like a procession of green lanterns moving through the fog. Only when the lights reach the shallows do their reflections reveal the broad bodies and the slow, careful placement of six feet beneath each glow.

Most of the light comes from living things: blue threads of algae in the water, amber fungi beneath the reefs, and the slow green pulses glowing inside the grazers themselves.

#### What it looks like

An adult lantern grazer is about the size of a rhinoceros, but much flatter and broader. Its body resembles a translucent turtle shell stretched over six jointed legs. Beneath its pearly skin, luminous organs flicker like lanterns behind frosted glass. When the animal is resting, these lights beat slowly. When it is frightened, they vanish at once.

Its back supports a forest of flexible, hollow spines, each as long as a human forearm. The spines are not weapons. They collect moisture from the air and channel it into grooves along the animal’s sides. In heavy fog, a grazer looks as though it is wearing a crown of glass reeds, each tipped with a trembling drop of water.

The six feet are wide, soft pads covered in thousands of tiny hooks. These let the animal cling to the floating reefs even when storms tip them almost vertically. A grazer can sleep upside down without falling.

Its head hangs beneath the front edge of its body. Instead of a face, it has a ring of four dark eyes surrounding a folded feeding fan. The eyes detect movement and the faintest glimmers of light, but they cannot form especially sharp images. To explore something unfamiliar, the grazer brushes it with two ribbonlike feelers that emerge beside its mouth.

Those feelers can taste minerals, sense heat, and pick up vibrations through the reef. A grazer can recognize a familiar animal by the rhythm of its footsteps long before it comes into view.

#### What it eats

Lantern grazers feed on the dense mats of microbial life that coat the undersides of Nacre’s reefs.

To eat, a grazer unfolds its feeding fan: a circular brush of fine, comb-shaped filaments. It presses the fan against the reef and sweeps it back and forth, gathering a mixture of algae, bacteria, and tiny shelled organisms. Hard particles are crushed by muscular plates deep in its throat.

Food is scarce, so almost nothing goes to waste. Its digestive tract contains several chambers filled with symbiotic microbes, each breaking down a different part of the meal. A single feeding session can sustain it for days.

Some of those microbes also inhabit specialized pockets beneath its skin. Supplied with nutrients and oxygen by the grazer, they produce its green light. The glow provides the microbes with a safe home and gives the grazer a means of communication.

Nacre’s days last nearly seventy Earth hours. Lantern grazers spend the brighter portion tucked into hollows along the reef’s edge, where their cloudy skin blends with pale mineral deposits. They hook their feet into place, withdraw their heads, and slow their breathing.

As darkness deepens, they emerge in loose groups of five to twenty.

They move slowly, testing each foothold before shifting their weight. On a quiet night, a herd makes a soft clicking sound as thousands of foot-hooks catch and release. Feeding animals usually keep a few body lengths apart, leaving enough space for each one to sweep its mouth across untouched reef.

Their lights carry simple messages. Two short green pulses mean that an animal is approaching closely. A long, dim glow helps a youngster follow its parent through murky water. At first glance, a glassback looks like a small hill walking through the fog.

It stands about as tall as a horse, but its body is broad and low, supported by six jointed legs. Each leg ends in a soft, circular foot that spreads under its weight, allowing it to cross Veyra’s floating marshes without breaking through. When it walks, its feet lift in alternating pairs, giving it a slow, rolling gait.

Its most striking feature is the translucent shell covering its back. The shell resembles smoky blue glass, with branching golden veins suspended inside it. Beneath the surface, bands of light drift and pulse—not reflections, but living colonies of tiny organisms housed within the shell. At night, a herd of glassbacks looks like a cluster of lanterns moving through the reeds.

The rest of the creature is less elegant. Its skin is charcoal-gray, thick, and deeply wrinkled, with a texture like wet tree bark. It has no obvious head. Instead, a flexible neck extends from the underside of its body, ending in a blunt feeding disk surrounded by twelve delicate feelers. Four glossy black eyes sit on short stalks around the shell’s front edge. These can turn independently, allowing the glassback to watch the sky while searching for food below.

### A world of dim light and deep marshes

Veyra circles a cool red star. Its daylight is weak and copper-colored, and its dense atmosphere holds moisture in almost permanent banks of fog. Much of the planet’s lowland surface consists of dark water covered by interwoven mats of vegetation. Some mats are thick enough to support forests; others tear beneath anything heavier than a bird.

Glassbacks live along the shifting boundaries between these floating islands.

Their broad feet sense pressure through thousands of fine hairs. Before committing their weight to a step, they press lightly against the ground and read the way the surrounding fibers stretch. Young glassbacks take months to master this skill. Adults sometimes reach a leg backward to steady a youngster crossing a thin patch.

If a glassback does fall through, it does not immediately drown. Air chambers beneath its shell keep it afloat, while its flattened legs paddle toward firmer ground. Getting back onto a vegetation mat, however, can take hours—and leaves its vulnerable underside exposed.

### How it feeds

A glassback eats the mineral-rich growths that form beneath marsh plants: soft fungal sheets, tangled roots, and colonies of small, tube-shaped animals.

Its feeding disk seals against a patch of vegetation and releases a warm digestive fluid. After several minutes, the food softens into a thick slurry, which the creature draws through a ring of small mouth openings. Its feelers sort edible material from sharp mineral deposits and remove parasites from around the mouth.

The organisms inside its shell also help feed it. During the day, they absorb the star’s dim light and produce sugars. In return, the glassback supplies them with water and nutrients carried through the shell’s golden channels. This partnership cannot sustain the animal by itself, but it helps it survive seasonal food shortages.

A healthy glassback glows softly turquoise after dark. A hungry one becomes dull blue. When sick, it may develop dark patches where its luminous partners have died.

### A quiet, social life

Glassbacks live in herds of eight to twenty individuals. They spend most of their time feeding, resting, and following well-established routes through the marsh.

They communicate in two ways. For nearby companions, they pulse the light beneath their shells in slow patterns. A ripple from front to back means “follow.” Three brief flashes signal alarm. During rest, members of a herd sometimes synchronize their glow, brightening and fading together over several minutes.

For distant communication, they press their bodies against the ground and produce deep vibrations using muscular plates beneath the chest. These tremors travel through the woven vegetation farther than sound carries through the thick fog. A glassback may detect an approaching herd long before it sees one.

They have good memories for safe crossings and seasonal feeding sites. Herds usually follow an older animal whose shell has grown cloudy with age. When a familiar path breaks apart in a storm, the leader probes for a new route while the others wait, sometimes for most of a day.

### Young beneath the shell

Once every few years, an adult grows a soft brood pouch beneath the rear edge of its shell. It lays two or three leathery eggs inside, where they remain warm and protected.

Newly hatched glassbacks are about the size of house cats. Their shells are flexible and almost transparent, revealing the slow movements of organs underneath. They are born without the luminous organisms that adults carry. During their first week, a parent rubs a secretion from its own shell across theirs, transferring the microscopic colonies.

For several months, the young cling to folds of skin beneath the parent’s body. They reach down to taste food while the adult feeds, then pull themselves back up at the slightest disturbance. As their shells harden, they begin walking beside the herd.

### What hunts it—and how it survives

The glassback’s main predator is a long-bodied marsh hunter called a veiljaw, which hides beneath floating vegetation and strikes upward.

An adult glassback is difficult to overturn. When threatened, it folds its neck and eye stalks beneath the shell, spreads its legs, and grips the vegetation with hooked ridges normally concealed inside its feet. The herd gathers around its young, forming a low wall of shells.

At the same time, the glassbacks produce a sudden burst of pale light. In Veyra’s dim environment, this can overwhelm a predator’s sensitive eyes long enough for the herd to retreat.

The flash is costly. It consumes reserves stored by the shell organisms, leaving the animals faintly lit for several nights afterward.

### The tracks it leaves behind

A glassback may live for seventy years. Its shell grows outward in subtle ridges, recording periods of abundance and hunger. Old individuals carry gardens of harmless mosslike organisms along their shell edges, sometimes with tiny animals nesting among them.

As glassbacks feed, they open narrow channels through the marsh mats, bringing water and dissolved nutrients into stagnant areas. Their droppings fertilize new growth, and their abandoned routes become waterways used by smaller creatures.

On a still Veyran night, a herd can be located by the faint glow beneath the fog and the soft sucking sounds of its feet. By morning it may be gone, leaving six parallel rows of shallow prints slowly filling with dark water.

Two flexible stalks rise behind its head. Their feathery tips detect airborne chemicals and small changes in temperature. When the animal is relaxed, these stalks droop. When alarmed, they stiffen and turn toward the disturbance.

Lanternbacks graze on **veilweed**, a black plant that grows in long sheets between rocks. Their mouths grip the edge of a sheet and draw it inward, where rows of hard ridges grind it into pulp.

Veilweed is tough and slow to digest. A lanternback’s abdomen contains three fermentation chambers filled with microorganisms that break down the fibers. After feeding, the animal often rests for hours with its legs folded beneath it. During these resting periods, small ripples pass along its sides as muscles shift food from one chamber to another.

It also seeks out mineral-rich clay beside rivers. The minerals help maintain its shell and the light-producing organs beneath it. Favorite clay banks become gathering places, worn smooth by generations of licking and scraping.

Its light is a form of communication.

Young lanternbacks have irregular, flickering lights. They must learn to control them, much as a young animal on Earth learns to coordinate its calls. A startled youngster may accidentally signal both “come closer” and “run,” causing a brief tangle of confused legs.

Light is especially useful in Orra’s dim, windy habitat, where calls are easily lost. Lanternbacks do make sounds, but mostly at close range: hollow clicks, low humming vibrations, and a dry rattle produced by rubbing two throat plates together.

Lanternbacks travel in herds of eight to twenty. They follow familiar routes through the twilight belt, moving between grazing grounds, mineral banks, and sheltered resting hollows.

The young first feed on a nutritious paste regurgitated by adults. This also supplies the microorganisms they need to digest veilweed. Feeding is shared across the herd, so a youngster may approach several adults before settling down to rest.

During the fiercest winds, a herd settles in the lee of a stone ridge. The adults fold their legs, tuck their heads beneath their shells, and reduce their glow to a faint green shimmer.

The young stay awake longer. They nose through the damp plants, inspect stones with their mouth-feelers, and practice tiny amber flashes. Occasionally, an adult answers with one slow pulse. The youngster edges closer, presses against its warm flank, and finally dims its light.

## The Lanternback of Veyra

At dusk on the alien planet Veyra, the forests begin to glow. Pale ribbons of light curl around the trunks of towering plants, and among their roots moves a creature like a walking tide pool: the **lanternback**.

### What it looks like

An adult lanternback is about the size of a small horse, but its body is low and broad, supported by six jointed legs. Each leg ends in three soft toes that can spread into a wide gripping pad. This lets it cross Veyra’s floating marshes without sinking and climb the slick, nearly vertical roots of the forest.

Its skin resembles frosted glass. Beneath it, faint blue and violet currents reveal the movement of its blood. A layer of flexible, overlapping plates protects its back. These plates are mostly transparent, and beneath each one sits a chamber filled with luminous microorganisms. In darkness, the chambers shine like a row of little aquariums.

A lanternback can brighten or dim each chamber separately. A frightened animal flashes white. A relaxed one glows soft green. During courtship, waves of amber light travel from its shoulders to the tip of its tail.

Its head is wedge-shaped, with four black eyes arranged in a shallow arc. The outer pair watch for movement; the inner pair focus on nearby objects. Under its chin hang two delicate feelers covered in silver hairs. These hairs detect chemicals in the air and vibrations in water, allowing the animal to find food even in thick fog.

Its mouth is hidden beneath a fold of skin. When feeding, it unfolds a broad, rasping tongue rather like a dark purple leaf.

### The world it inhabits

Veyra is a cool, damp planet beneath a reddish sun. Its dense atmosphere carries sound unusually well, and its weaker gravity allows the forest’s plantlike organisms to grow into vast, branching towers. Their roots form tangled platforms above shallow mineral-rich seas.

The lanternback lives where these root platforms meet the water. The ground is rarely stable: mats of vegetation rise with the tides, split apart in storms, and slowly drift. A creature that depends on a permanent trail would soon become lost.

Instead, lanternbacks remember patterns of scent and vibration. They can recognize a feeding grove by the low creak of its roots or find a sheltered nesting hollow by the particular mineral taste of the water around it.

### What it eats

Lanternbacks graze on thick microbial films that grow along submerged roots. They brace themselves with four legs, use the front pair to turn over loose vegetation, and scrape food away with their textured tongues.

The films contain both nutrients and tiny luminous organisms. Some of those organisms survive digestion and enter special channels leading to the chambers beneath the lanternback’s plates. There, the animal supplies them with sugars and oxygen; in return, they produce light.

Keeping this living light system healthy takes considerable energy. During lean seasons, a lanternback’s glow becomes patchy, then nearly disappears. Healthy adults sometimes leave the richest feeding patches to their young, whose light chambers are still developing.

They also eat soft, balloon-shaped fruits that fall from the forest canopy. Fermented fruits make them sleepy and clumsy, so older lanternbacks test each one with a chin feeler before biting it. Youngsters are less cautious.

### How it spends its days

During daylight, lanternbacks sleep in groups beneath overhanging roots. They fold their legs tightly under their bodies and turn their armored backs outward. A sleeping group looks like a cluster of wet stones.

At twilight, they wake and exchange slow pulses of light. These signals communicate simple but important things: *I am here. Follow me. Keep your distance. There is danger.*

A typical group contains six to twelve animals. They are social without being tightly coordinated. One may wander away to investigate a scent, while another spends an hour scratching algae from a companion’s back plates. Their grooming keeps the plates clear enough for light signals to remain visible.

They also communicate through the ground. By tapping their front feet against a root, they send vibrations farther than their glow can be seen. A quick sequence of heavy taps warns the group of a predator.

### How it survives

The lanternback’s chief predator is the sailjaw, a long-bodied glider that drops from the canopy. Against attacks from above, the lanternback’s overlapping back plates act as flexible armor.

If a sailjaw approaches, the lanternback first freezes and extinguishes its lights. Its gray-green skin blends with the wet roots. If concealment fails, every light chamber flashes at once. In Veyra’s dark understory, that burst can briefly overwhelm the predator’s sensitive eyes.

The lanternback then dives into water. Small breathing slits along its sides seal shut, while oxygen stored in its blood allows it to remain submerged for nearly twenty minutes. Its toes fold backward, and its broad tail becomes a paddle.

As a last resort, it releases a cloud of glowing mucus. The cloud hangs in the water while the animal escapes into darkness. Replacing the mucus is costly, so a lanternback that has used this defense usually spends the next few nights feeding rather than traveling.

### Raising its young

Once every three local years, groups gather around warm mineral springs. Females lay three or four leathery eggs in pockets of damp vegetation above the waterline. Adults take turns resting beside the nests, protecting them from scavengers and keeping the nesting material moist.

Newly hatched lanternbacks are hand-sized and completely dark. Their back plates are soft, and their toes are disproportionately large, making them look as though they are wearing oversized gloves.

Their first meal is a special mucus produced by the adults. It contains the microorganisms needed to seed their light chambers. After several days, a faint blue point appears beneath the first plate. More lights develop over the following months.

Young lanternbacks learn signals by imitation. They often flash at the wrong moment—announcing danger at a falling fruit or sending a courtship pattern while asking for food. Adults respond with gentle nudges and repeated, slower signals.

### Its place in the forest

As lanternbacks graze, they prevent microbial growth from smothering the forest roots. Seeds caught between their toes travel to new root islands, while nutrients in their droppings feed small floating gardens.

Their lights have also become part of the nightly rhythm of the marsh. Tiny flying animals follow feeding groups to catch insects disturbed by their movements. Some harmless scavengers even produce lanternback-like flashes, encouraging the larger animals to tolerate them nearby.

On a quiet Veyran night, a group crossing the marsh looks like a constellation moving beneath the trees. Every so often, one light stops, brightens, and waits—until a smaller, unsteady glow catches up.

On Namarra, a planet lit by a dim orange sun, forests grow beneath a permanent layer of fog. Their trunks are black, their leaves broad and silver, and their roots reach into warm underground rivers. A glassback has a low, oval body supported by six long legs. Each leg ends in three soft, spreading toes that grip wet roots without breaking their delicate bark. It moves slowly but rarely stumbles: even when stepping over a fallen tree, it keeps four feet firmly planted.

Its shell resembles smoky green glass. Beneath it, branching tissues pulse with pale blue light, while clusters of tiny amber nodules brighten and fade as the animal breathes. The shell is not perfectly smooth. Shallow grooves channel condensed fog toward the creature’s mouth.

Instead of a distinct head, the glassback has a flexible neck ending in a flat, shovel-shaped face. Four dark eyes sit along its upper edge. Two look forward, judging distance; the other two watch overhead for predators concealed in the canopy. A fringe of fine sensory threads hangs beneath its jaw. These threads detect vibration, moisture, and traces of chemicals left by other animals.

Its mouth is a narrow slit containing overlapping mineral plates. They let it scrape food from stone and bark with a faint sound like a spoon drawn across pottery.

The most striking part of a glassback is visible through its shell: delicate violet fronds growing in fluid-filled chambers along its spine. These are living partners, somewhat like algae, that share the animal’s body.

#### How it feeds

The violet organisms use Namarra’s weak sunlight to make sugars. They supply enough energy to keep a resting glassback alive, but not enough for walking, growing, or raising young.

To supplement this food, the animal eats mineral-rich fungal mats, soft roots, and the rubbery fruit that drops from the forest canopy. Its sensory fringe can distinguish ripe fruit buried beneath mud from fruit that has begun to produce poisonous defensive chemicals.

At midday, glassbacks climb exposed ridges and spread thin folds of skin from beneath their shells. These folds act as additional light collectors. A resting herd looks like a gathering of green stones surrounded by translucent purple fans.

Their diet also repairs their armor. Specialized glands extract minerals from food and deposit them in the shell, slowly sealing scratches and cracks. An old glassback carries cloudy seams where injuries have healed.

#### How it senses the world

Namarra’s fog makes distant vision unreliable, so glassbacks depend heavily on sound conducted through the ground.

They communicate by pressing their throats against roots and producing low vibrations. A forest’s interconnected root network carries these signals much farther than a call would travel through the air. Other glassbacks listen through sensitive pads in their feet.

Their messages are simple but useful: danger nearby, good feeding ground, a missing youngster, or an invitation to gather.

Within a herd, individuals also recognize one another by the rhythm of the lights beneath their shells. Young animals flash rapidly when excited. Adults glow more slowly, and a frightened glassback abruptly goes dark.

#### Where it sleeps

At night, the forest becomes cold enough for the fog to freeze on exposed branches. Glassbacks shelter in hollows near the warm rivers beneath the soil.

Before sleeping, an animal folds its legs tightly under its shell and draws its face into a protective collar. It then releases a sticky substance around the shell’s lower rim, fastening itself to the ground. This seal conserves warmth and prevents small burrowing parasites from reaching its softer underside.

A sleeping glassback looks like a dimly illuminated boulder. Its internal lights continue to flicker, though no one knows whether those patterns correspond to dreams.

#### Predators and defenses

Its main predator is the hookwing, a canopy-dwelling hunter that drops onto animals from above. Hookwings try to flip glassbacks over, exposing the unarmored belly.

A glassback’s first defense is stillness. Its translucent shell takes on the colors of the wet vegetation around it, making it difficult to distinguish from a moss-covered rock.

If discovered, it braces its six legs and releases a sharp burst of light from beneath its shell. In the dim forest, this can briefly dazzle a predator. At the same time, it stamps a warning into the roots.

Nearby adults respond by gathering around the youngest members of the herd, their shells touching. A hookwing can overturn a lone youngster, but it struggles to find a grip on this continuous wall of armor.

#### How it raises its young

Glassbacks lay two or three leathery eggs in warm mineral mud. The parents take turns guarding the nest and keeping the eggs damp with water collected in their shell grooves.

Hatchlings emerge pale and almost completely transparent. They have no violet fronds inside them yet. During their first week, they feed on a nutrient-rich secretion produced beneath a parent’s neck. That secretion contains the tiny organisms that will grow into their internal gardens.

For several months, the young travel beneath the adults’ bodies. Their short legs let them scurry between the larger animals’ feet, and their frequent blue flashes help parents keep track of them in the fog.

A glassback may live for sixty local years. As it ages, its shell thickens and becomes less transparent, reducing the light that reaches its violet partners. Elderly animals spend more time on sunny ridges and depend increasingly on food gathered from the ground.

#### Its place in the forest

Glassbacks carry fungal spores between distant valleys and loosen compacted soil with their broad toes. Their droppings return valuable minerals to the forest floor.

Even their abandoned shells remain useful. After a glassback dies, its shell can persist for decades, filling with rainwater and becoming a sheltered pool for tiny aquatic creatures. Seedlings sometimes take root inside the cracked armor.

On Namarra, a young tree growing out of a green, glassy bowl is often the last trace of an animal that once walked through the fog.

### The Lanternback of Veyra

At dusk on the planet Veyra, the forests begin to glow—and some of the lights move.

They belong to lanternbacks: six-legged creatures about the size of a pony, with translucent skin, broad leaf-shaped ears, and a branching crown of luminous organs along their spines. Seen through the permanent mist, a wandering herd resembles a constellation drifting between the trees.

#### What it looks like

A lanternback’s body is low and long, supported by six flexible legs. Each foot spreads into four soft pads that grip wet stone and distribute its weight across Veyra’s floating moss beds. It moves in an alternating rhythm, keeping three feet planted while the other three step forward. Even at a run, it scarcely seems to bounce.

Its skin is pale gray in daylight, with a faint green tint from microscopic organisms living just beneath the surface. Across its flanks, you can see darker shapes: looping blood vessels, sheets of muscle, and the slow contractions of its digestive chambers. When threatened, it floods its outer skin with dark pigment, becoming opaque and difficult to spot among the roots.

Its head is blunt and wedge-shaped. Four glossy eyes sit beneath a protective ridge: two look forward to judge distance, while two smaller eyes watch overhead. A fringe of sensitive tendrils surrounds its mouth. These taste the air and test food before a pair of tough, beaklike plates clips it free.

The “lanterns” along its back are hollow, branching structures filled with luminous microbes. An adult usually has seven, although their shapes are as individual as fingerprints. Muscular valves regulate the oxygen reaching the microbes, allowing the animal to brighten or dim each lantern separately.

#### Its strange home

Veyra circles a dim red star. Its atmosphere is dense, its gravity slightly weaker than Earth’s, and much of its surface is covered by shallow, warm wetlands. Towering organisms resembling a mixture of trees and coral rise from the water. Their interlocking branches support mats of vegetation thick enough for lanternbacks to walk across.

The ground is rarely dependable. A patch of moss might conceal solid roots, deep water, or a pocket of gas.

Before putting its full weight on a foot, a lanternback sends a faint vibration through the pads and listens through sensitive structures in its leg joints. The returning tremors help it distinguish a sturdy branch from a thin mat over open water. Young animals occasionally misjudge a crossing, but they float well: air sacs along their ribs keep their heads above water while they paddle toward firmer ground.

#### What it eats

Lanternbacks feed mostly on ribbonlike plants that hang beneath the forest canopy. They pull these ribbons down with their mouth tendrils, clip off small portions, and grind them between ridged plates deeper in the jaw.

Their food is fibrous and contains irritating mineral crystals, so digestion is slow. Three stomach chambers hold communities of microbes that break down the fibers and neutralize much of the plant’s chemical defenses. The indigestible crystals become compact pellets, which the animal periodically coughs up.

They also scrape mineral-rich crusts from old trunks. These provide salts needed by both the lanternback and its glowing microbes.

The green organisms beneath its skin contribute a little extra nourishment through photosynthesis. On brighter days, lanternbacks spread their broad ears toward the sky and rest for hours. Sunlight cannot sustain them by itself, but it helps them survive when food is scarce.

#### How it lives with others

Lanternbacks travel in herds of eight to twenty, usually led by an older female familiar with the safest routes through the wetlands.

They communicate through a combination of light, posture, and low sounds. A slow ripple of blue-green light from neck to tail means that a feeding area is safe. Three quick flashes signal alarm. A steady glow from the rearmost lantern helps younger animals follow through thick fog.

Their ears detect deep calls that carry well through Veyra’s dense air. Nearby, these calls sound less like voices than like someone drawing a wet finger around the rim of an enormous glass.

Herd members greet one another by touching mouth tendrils. This lets them recognize scent, assess health, and exchange some of the microbes essential to digestion. An animal returning after a long absence may be inspected by every member of the herd before being allowed to settle among them.

At rest, the adults form a loose ring around the young. They do not all sleep at once. A resting lanternback folds four legs beneath its body but leaves its front pair braced, ready to lift its head at the slightest unfamiliar vibration.

#### Raising its young

Once every three local years, a female lays one large, leathery egg in a nest woven from stripped plant ribbons. The nest hangs just above the water, where temperatures remain relatively stable.

For several weeks, adults take turns guarding it. They warm the egg by curling around it and cool it by wetting the nest.

A hatchling emerges nearly transparent, with oversized feet and only small bumps where its lanterns will grow. Its first meals come from a nutrient-rich secretion produced by the parent’s mouth glands. This secretion also supplies the microbes that will colonize its stomach and lantern organs.

Young lanternbacks cannot control their lights very well. They often glow brightly when excited or hungry, making them conspicuous targets. Adults shelter them beneath their bodies during dangerous crossings. By the end of their first year, the young can dim themselves and produce the herd’s basic signals.

#### Staying alive

Their main predator is the sailmaw, a quiet glider that drops from the upper canopy. The lanternback’s upward-facing eyes help detect its silhouette, but mist often hides an approaching attack.

When one herd member spots danger, its alarm flashes pass rapidly through the group. The adults crowd together, keeping their backs outward and the young beneath them. Their lantern branches look delicate, but each contains a sharp, mineralized core that makes landing on them hazardous.

If caught alone, a lanternback extinguishes its lights, darkens its skin, and presses itself against a trunk. As a last resort, it can shed the glowing tip of a lantern. The detached tip continues to shine for several minutes, sometimes drawing a predator away while the animal escapes. Regrowing it takes months.

#### Its place in the forest

Lanternbacks carry seeds in their digestive tracts and scatter them along the routes they follow. Their feeding opens gaps in dense vegetation, while their mineral pellets slowly dissolve into the wetlands, supplying nutrients to smaller organisms.

Old lanternbacks leave especially deep trails through the moss. After decades of use, these paths become narrow channels where water flows and new plants take root.

A herd may abandon a route when a great supporting branch finally collapses. Yet long afterward, its passage remains visible from above: a winding seam of young growth through the dark forest, tracing the journeys of animals whose lights have moved elsewhere.
